newsitem.title: UK: European fuel seen climbing again from 5-year high.
newsitem.headline: European fuel seen climbing again from 5-year high.

text.p: European fuel oil looks likely to rise further this winter despite having already hit five-year highs, traders said.
Rotterdam heavy fuel barges, widely regarded as the European benchmark, traded at $126 a tonne on Thursday, the highest level since January 1991 during the height of the Gulf War.
Low stocks of heavy fuel oil in the big Western consuming nations, growing winter demand and cheap prices versus other markets are all likely to drive prices higher, traders said.

"It looks well supported at these levels and could well go higher. I wouldn't be surprised to see it hit the $130 level on cargoes," said Glenn Murray of Starsupply in Monaco, a leading fuel brokerage.
Heavy fuel storage tanks in Europe and the U.S. are languishing around eight percent below year ago levels at a critical time of the year.

Russian exports, which usually replenish European tanks during the summer, failed to hit last year's levels in May, June and July, traders say. This left many Rotterdam dealers struggling to find supplies from local refiners, although Russian exports did pick up in August. But as winter approaches, Russian material will be kept increasingly for domestic use and less will be exported.
Winter demand for fuel is already beginning to pick up. Romania has earmarked $160 million to buy fuel over the next few months, which means about 1.2 million tonnes at current prices.

Power companies in the U.K., Ireland and Portugal are also likely to buy soon, traders said. The world's biggest fuel oil buyer, Italian state power company Enel, is playing its cards close to its chest.

It has managed to avoid buying spot cargoes for much of this year by running down its huge stockpile of oil while also burning more gas and coal. Some traders are sceptical whether it can hold out for the whole winter without dipping back onto the spot market.
Enel burns some 23 million tonnes of fuel oil a year, of which some three million is sourced from the spot market.

At the end of September stocks of fuel oil in Italy, which combines Enel and the oil industry, were nearly 400,000 tonnes below year ago levels. The high absolute price of fuel may have delayed purchases among some buyers who had hoped for weaker levels.
Prices above $120 a tonne in Rotterdam "tend to discourage some buyers," said Jim McLaren of Alimar BV in Rotterdam.
But the delays may have a sting in the tail if buyers stampede at a later date, he added.

Compared with other markets European fuel oil remains cheap. Rotterdam barges are about $4.80 a barrel cheaper than Brent crude which costs around $24.12 a barrel for IPE front month futures. But over the past year it has averaged just $3.55 less than Brent, slipping to current low levels when it failed to keep up with sharp gains on Brent since the end of June.
This time last year the fuel discount to front month Brent was $2.50.

As well as being cheap against Brent, European fuel oil is likely to enjoy some support from Asian and U.S. markets which are roughly at parity with Rotterdam. --Matthew Jones, Sam Arnold-Forster, London Newsroom, +44 171 542 8980
